title: Detecting Hidden ML Training With Zero-Overhead Telemetry
claim: Classifiers transfer reliably between similar hardware but degrade across hardware classes, while leave-one-out evaluation still generalizes to unseen devices.
layout: 1 panel, train-by-test matrix with a separated bottom summary row
description: A single large heatmap. Rows are the training GPU: RTX 4050 Laptop, RTX 5080, RTX 5090, A100 40GB, A100 80GB, H100 80GB, H100 NVL, H200 and B200. Columns are the test GPU in the same order. Each cell shows an accuracy percentage and is coloured on a red-yellow-green scale from 0.5 to 1.0, with a colorbar on the right. A thick black line separates the main 9x9 grid from a bottom row labelled Leave-one-GPU-out, which is nearly all dark green at 100%. Datacenter rows such as H200 and B200 are mostly dark green. Consumer rows and some A100 and H100 rows contain scattered red and orange cells, with values in the 30s to 50s. The eye goes first to the red cells against the green background.
caption: Cross-GPU transfer heatmap (binary RF, 30\,s windows). Cell values are accuracy when training on the row GPU and testing on the column GPU. Datacenter-to-datacenter transfer is consistently above 90%. Cross-consumer and consumer$\leftrightarrow$datacenter transfer is weaker; RTX 4050/5080/5090 rows often drop below 50% on datacenter targets. The bottom row is LOGO: for each test GPU, the classifier is trained only on data from the other 8 GPUs. By contrast, in-distribution evaluation (with runs from the target GPU included in the training dataset) reaches 100% on unseen non-adversarial runs, for every GPU. LOGO evaluates the harder case of generalization to new hardware types.
abstract: Hardware-enabled monitoring of GPU workloads underpins many proposals for AI compute governance, but if developers can defeat monitoring mechanisms, such schemes are unworkable. We evaluate the adversarial robustness of GPU workload classification using only zero-overhead, privacy-preserving NVML telemetry: content-agnostic signals that observe physical effects of computation without accessing model weights, training data, or hyperparameters. Across 5 rounds of monitor-evader iteration, we evaluate 20 evasion strategy families on 9 GPU models spanning 4 architecture generations. We develop a classifier that achieves 98.2% binary accuracy at identifying training workloads across the whole corpus, and 43-87% accuracy against the most challenging unexpected workloads even when they are adversarially disguised.
